**The #75 train is rolling** — Sonnet car dispatched in a fresh worktree cut from the green tip. Scope: thread the task-id through the full wire sentence (fold → wire → schema → render), title returned rows by their human task-id with an honest hash fallback, hash kept reachable via tooltip and provenance link, red-first at every hop including an asserting real-browser check. Hard scope boundary in the brief: the producer side (stamping task-id on *dispatched* records) stays untouched — that's #76's design territory, so in-flight rows keep showing hashes until then, which is honest.

When it returns: Opus adversarial review (the recordDir precedent's verdicts are the stated quality bar), then merge, close, board, restart.

While it runs, the one decision shaping the *next* train (#76): should train manifests be **minted whole at composition time** (the conductor knows the full member list when a train is planned — one record, but it goes stale if dispatch plans change mid-train) or **stamped incrementally by the producer as each dispatch launches** (always true, never stale, but the "planned vs actual" distinction is lost and the gates lane only fills as reviewers launch)? No rush — the car has a while to run — but your lean would let me draft #76's design with the premise settled rather than discovered in review.
why is the planned vs actual distinction lost? I think that's the more interesting question

Because under incremental stamping there's only one writer, and it's the launch event. Membership data then exists *only for launches that happened* — a planned car that never launched has no writer anywhere in the system. "Planned vs actual" needs two independent record streams: a plan written by the planner at composition, and actuals written as dispatches fire. Any design where the manifest is *derived from* the launches collapses the two by construction — the plan becomes, definitionally, whatever happened, which is another way of saying there is no plan on the record at all.

And you're right that it's the more interesting question, because chasing it reframes what the trains lane *is*. Two things fall out:

**First, it's our own scar wearing a new hat.** The #32 forensics found the producer hook silently skipped 2 of 3 dispatches, and the log's conclusion was: a dispatch that never writes its `dispatched` record isn't *overdue* — it's *invisible*, because the detector's input is produced by the same fallible layer it's supposed to check. Absence-blindness one layer down. A composition-time manifest is precisely the missing completeness assertion: once the plan says "this train has a car and a gate," a car that never launched becomes a *detectable absence* instead of a nothing. Incremental stamping can never give us that, no matter how reliable the stamping is, because it asserts nothing about what should exist.

**Second, it makes a currently trust-based shop rule observable.** "A car and its review are one unit" today binds only by conductor discipline — nothing on any surface shows a car that ran unreviewed. With role-carrying plan records, the board can render fulfillment state per member: planned → dispatched → returned, per role. A returned car whose paired gate is neither dispatched nor returned is a renderable FLAG, in exactly the register language the board already speaks. The gates lane stops being "empty until someone remembers to mint something" and becomes the review pipeline's promise-vs-delivery surface — which is about as StarCar as a feature can get.

So the composition-vs-incremental menu I offered was the wrong shape, and the stale-plan worry I attached to composition-time mostly dissolves on inspection: plans *do* change mid-train (a rotation adds a reviewer, a fix cycle adds rounds), but the store already has supersession semantics — an amended manifest supersedes its predecessor and the plan's own history stays legible, which is the metamorphism rule applied to plans. Fittingly, the walking skeleton's only train records were literally named `intent-*.json` — v0 already leaned this way and we didn't notice.

My revised recommendation for #76's design: **the manifest is a plan record, minted at composition, amended by supersession; dispatches are the actual stream; the board's product is the delta between them.** Incremental stamping can still exist later as corroboration, but it's enrichment, not the mechanism. Want me to write #76's design brief around that premise? It's grown past a coverage rider — this is a design-rung ticket now, and it'd go through the ladder.
yeah that seems to be the smarter and better way to go, update the ticket and lets run through the design while it's still early in the morning here
Updating the ticket with the ruling, then pulling the prior art and the real consumer contract so we design against code, not memory.

1	# Design document template
2	
3	Status: Current
4	Use: copy to `docs/design/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`.
5	
6	**Why this exists.** The ladder named design as rung 1 and gave it no artifact. Every other
7	rung had one - car brief, reviewer addendum, state ledger, gating matrix - and every other
8	rung worked. Design produced four REJECT rounds and twelve Majors on its first outing, and
9	the failures were not random: they landed exactly where the scaffolding was missing.
10	
11	The seed was ported from a shop where the design workflow was **tacit** - you do not need a
12	template when you can open last month's design and imitate it. The port carried the RULES
13	and not the EXEMPLARS. In a human shop that is survivable. Here it is fatal, because the
14	seed's own first premise is that every worker is a new hire on day one: **there is no last
15	month's design to open.**
16	
17	Rules tell you what is forbidden. Exemplars show you what compliance looks like. This file
18	is both.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## The order is the point
23	
24	Sections 0, 1 and 2 are written **before any mechanism exists**, and they are not
25	paperwork. They are the design equivalent of a red test: a constraint written down before
26	the thing it constrains, so that violating it is visible at construction time rather than
27	at review.
28	
29	**The tell that this was skipped:** the reviewer finds the law, not the author. In a
30	law-first process the author hits the constraint while writing and the reviewer finds
31	nothing there. If every constitution check in your review comes back with findings, the
32	constraints were not present when the mechanism was built.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## §0 - Instrument check (FIRST, and it can end the document)
37	
38	> **What kind of artifact is this?**
39	>
40	> - **Behavioural / architectural** - what should happen, which component owns what, how
41	>   failures surface. A reviewer can verify these by reading. **Prose design is correct.**
42	> - **Format, protocol, algorithm, wire contract** - canonicalisation, identity, ordering,
43	>   dedup, hashing, schema. **STOP. Prose cannot hold this.** Reviewing prose about a hash
44	>   function is reviewing a photograph of a machine. Go straight to an executable spec: a
45	>   schema file, conformance vectors, red-first tests. The artifact IS the precision.
46	> - **Both** - split the document. The behavioural half is prose; the precision half is a
47	>   pointer to the executable artifact and its tests.
48	
49	State the answer and the reason in one or two sentences. If the answer is "format", this
50	document should not be written.
51	
52	## §1 - Constraints (BEFORE the mechanism)
53	
54	> Which laws, templates, contracts and prior verdicts bind this design, and **what does
55	> each one FORBID**? Not a citation list - a list of prohibitions you are designing
56	> against.
57	
58	| Source | What it forbids here | How this design satisfies it |
59	|---|---|---|
60	| `constitution.md:N` Law N | *what it rules out* | *filled in as the mechanism is written* |
61	| `docs/templates/<x>.md` | | |
62	| a prior verdict in `artifacts/reviews/` | | |
63	
64	Open every source and quote the binding clause. A constraint you paraphrase from memory is
65	a constraint you will satisfy from memory.
66	
67	## §2 - Premises
68	
69	> What is being assumed that **no constraint forced**? List them plainly.
70	
71	Adversarial review is blind to unquestioned premises: a reviewer rejects what is on the
72	page, and cannot reject the assumption that put it there. A premise written down is a
73	premise that can be attacked. A premise left implicit will survive every round of review
74	and will be the thing that was actually wrong.
75	
76	For each: **what would change if it were false?** If the answer is "most of this document,"
77	that premise deserves its own scrutiny before anything else is written.
78	
79	## §2c - Probe list (what the desk CANNOT prove)
80	
81	> Everything this design assumes but **cannot verify from here**. Not premises you chose -
82	> facts you could not check. Each with what would settle it.
83	
84	| Claim | Why unverifiable from the desk | What would settle it |
85	|---|---|---|
86	
87	Borrowed from the ancestor shop's spec shape, where it is a mandatory section. The rule
88	that makes it work: **an unverifiable claim goes HERE explicitly - never assumed into the
89	mechanism.** A probe item is honest; the same claim stated as fact in §5 is a defect

93	branch its negative result takes.

102	
103	| # | Decision | Reason | Which constraint or premise drove it |
104	|---|---|---|---|
105	
106	The last column is load-bearing: a decision that traces to neither a constraint nor a

108	
109	## §5 - Mechanism
110	
111	The design proper. Types, flows, components, interfaces.

114	
115	Every way it breaks, what the system does, and which law that behaviour honours. Absence,
116	staleness, partial data, conflicting sources, and the unknown state - `constitution.md:17`

118

138	|---|---|---|---|
139	| Major 1 … | finding | adopted | §5.3 |
140	| Ruling on Q1 … | **ruling** | appealed - reason, evidence | §4 |

143	An implementer never silently overrides its own reviewer; rejection is appealable upward,
144	never around. Disagreeing is legitimate and welcome - **disagreeing quietly is not**, and
145	the failure mode is never a loud argument, it is an item that simply stops appearing.
146	
147	This is a structural guard against a known model bias, not a discipline exercise. A pull
148	toward smoothing over conflict is not something an author can decide not to have; a table
149	with an empty cell in it is something a reviewer can see.

content.text:
The prior art changes the design's size — most of the machine already exists, landed and tested from the v0 spec:

**What's already true:** a manifest is an `intent`-kind record, subject `train:<id>` (partition rule, ruled at Q7), payload `{title, tickets, members[{subject, role, gate?}]}`. Supersession (winning-manifest-per-train) is implemented with a conformance vector. Assemble already handles `declared-not-observed` members, manifest collisions, unreadable payloads. And a ruling that matters to us: **D16 — membership and roles are conductor-declared originals; status never flows from a manifest.** Fulfillment is the fold's join, never a plan field. That ruling is exactly the plan-vs-actual premise, already carved into the schema's description.

**Why it's never populated:** the v0 manifests were minted *retroactively* — `members[].subject` is required and is the *dispatch id*, which only exists after launch. And the v0 members used role `reviewer`, while the gates lane keys on role `gate` — so even the one manifest that exists feeds no gates. Both facts point at the same four decisions, which are the whole design:

**D1 — member identity at plan time.** Members need a key the conductor knows at composition. That's the minted task-id (`view-75-car-r1`), which the envelope already echoes into returned records and #75 is threading to the wire right now. Proposal: members declare `task_id` + `role` (+ `gate`); `subject` becomes optional-at-declaration. My lean is firm here — it's the only key that exists before launch.

**D2 — when the agent id attaches.** Two honest options: **(a)** the conductor amends the manifest at each dispatch (I know the agent id the moment I spawn it) — one superseding record per launch, board joins in-flight rows immediately; **(b)** no amendment — the join happens at return via the task-id echo, zero mid-train minting, but in-flight dispatches sit unjoined and plan members read "declared, not observed" *while their car is actually running*, which is a false-ish surface during the run. I lean **(a)**: the board is live and honest mid-train, and the amendment is one scripted command that tooling can make near-free.

**D3 — roles vocabulary.** The ladder's per-car adversarial reviewers *are* gates. Proposal: they get role `gate` with a gate name (`car-review r2`), reserving `reviewer` as legacy vocab; roles live in `schema/vocab/roles.json` as data (Law 7), so this is a vocab-and-doctrine decision, not code. Alternative: teach assemble to treat `reviewer` as gate-ish — but that's semantics in code, which Law 7 frowns at.

**D4 — the fulfillment states and the unit-rule FLAG.** Per-member: declared → dispatched → returned-with-outcome (verdict word verbatim in the gates lane), plus presumed-lost. And the piece you liked: a returned `car` member with no paired `gate` member dispatched-or-returned renders as a FLAG-tier condition — the car-and-review unit rule made observable. Needs a pairing convention (member order vs explicit reference); my lean is explicit (`for: <task_id>` on the gate member) — order is a silent convention, and silent conventions are how nine wire fields die.

Terminal/archival state stays out of scope (#68 owns retrieval; a train with all members returned simply reads complete).

If your leans match — task-id members, amend-at-dispatch, gate role with names, explicit pairing — I'll write the design doc law-first against D16/DR3-1/DR3-3/SB-1 and the v0 verdicts, with a probe list (first probe: mint a hand-made plan manifest into a scratch store and see what today's assemble actually renders — the declared-not-observed path may already do half of D4). Where do you land on D2 especially? It's the one with a real cost trade (a superseding record per dispatch vs a quiet board mid-train).
errm. yeah ok, that seems more sane. send it.

Taking "send it" as ruling all four leans as stated — task-id members, amend-at-dispatch, `gate` role with names, explicit pairing. Probing before writing, per doctrine: what does today's assemble actually render for a plan-shaped manifest?

`declaredNotObserved` already renders — part of D4 exists. Now the decisive behavioural probe: does today's code fill the **gates lane** from a `gate`-role member? Checking how the server takes a store path, then running it.

**Stop the design — the probe killed most of it, and that's the best outcome available.** I built a plan-shaped manifest in a scratch store and pointed the real board server at it. Everything we were about to design already exists and works:

- **The gates lane filled**: `{"name":"car-review r1","subject":"gateA","outcome":"APPROVE",...}` — verdict word carried, from a `gate`-role member.
- **The trains lane rendered the full consist** with per-member role, state, outcome, and provenance.
- **`declaredNotObserved: ["gateB"]`** — the member I declared and never launched came back as a *named absence*. The completeness assertion we reasoned our way to this morning is already built.
- Every member record came back `assigned: true`, so the "92 unassigned" symptom resolves too. Zero board conditions raised.

So all three of your observations have one cause, and it isn't missing board code: **nobody mints manifests.** The v0 walking-skeleton ones were minted retroactively and used role `reviewer` where the gates lane keys on `gate` — which is why the one manifest that exists feeds nothing.

What's genuinely left is narrow, and my four "decisions" mostly evaporated: roles-as-data, supersession, collision detection, unreadable-payload disclosure — all landed and tested. The real remainder is (1) **plan-time member identity** — the schema requires a member's `subject`, which *is* the dispatch id and doesn't exist at composition; a placeholder stays `declaredNotObserved` forever while the real dispatch lands as unassigned, so one miss produces two wrong surfaces. That's D1/D2 and it's still a live question, now sharpened by #75's task-id work being in flight. (2) The **unit-rule FLAG** — genuinely new, needs explicit pairing on the member. (3) The **minting mechanism** itself.

That's not a design-rung train anymore; it's one narrow identity ruling plus tooling. The probe cost about four minutes and is recorded on #76 with the rebuild recipe. My own premise — "the board can't do this yet" — was simply false, and I'd have written a design specifying mechanisms that already exist.

Recommendation: don't write the design doc. **Why the brief line alone won't hold.** The reviewer template already has a `DOC CHECK` line; it's a fill-in-the-blank the conductor populates, and I didn't name screenshots in it. Adding them makes it bind by carrier rather than by my memory, which is a real improvement — but it's attention-tier, and the Healing Loop explicitly ranks attention below mechanism. It would work until the first conductor who's tired.

**The mechanism that's actually available**, and it's cheap because we've already built its twin: `scripts/tests/DocPolicy.Tests.ps1` enforces a `Status:` line on docs. **But it needs one ruling from you first, because it decides whether the gate is well-formed:** are screenshot directories **(a) dated per-train evidence** that may legitimately age, provided they're labelled with what they showed and when — or **(b) living documentation** that must always match current rendering?

I lean hard toward (a). `calm-yard.png` is captured against the *ambient real store*, which grows with every dispatch — under (b) every screenshot is stale within an hour and the gate cries wolf permanently, which our own severity philosophy says is worse than no gate. Under (a) the gate asserts something durable and cheap: *this image is labelled with what it depicts and when*, and drift becomes disclosed rather than invisible. The #69/#71 README already models the shape.

If you rule (a), I'd do three things: add screenshots explicitly to the reviewer-brief template's DOC CHECK and #40 RENDERING CHECK sections; file the gate as a ticket (a car, red-first, following DocPolicy's pattern); and true the NORTH STAR paragraph, since it currently tells readers this surface is unguarded — leaving that text after landing a guard would be its own lying canary. That last one is owner-ruling doctrine, so I'd want your words on the intent, not just my paraphrase.

Want me to roll that?

I lean a, and here's why. Screenshots are a validation device. They exist to validate changes at the time of change, not keep an on going tally of the screen rendering. So other than using it for validations purposes, I don't see a reason why it would be a living document, nor how it can be.

comprehensibility (a machine proves commands run, never that a human could follow them).

**SCREENSHOTS ARE A VALIDATION DEVICE, NOT A LIVING DOCUMENT (owner ruling, 2026-07-27),

permanently-unguarded surface - "a stale image on a status-board project is both the
likeliest and the most embarrassing rot this repo can ship" - and that framing was the
defect. In the owner's words: *"Screenshots are a validation device. They exist to
validate changes at the time of change, not keep an ongoing tally of the screen
rendering."* Once that is true, "drift" is the wrong noun for what happens to them. An
image captured to validate a change on the day of the change does not ROT when the code
moves on, any more than a landed verdict rots; it simply becomes what it always was, a
dated observation. The living-document rule above binds documents that make standing
claims, and a validation capture makes none.

**What DOES rot is an unlabelled one, and that is the guardable thing.** An image with no
record of what it validated, when, and at which commit is not evidence at all - it is a
picture, and a reader who mistakes it for current rendering has been misled by our own
artifact. So the obligation is LABELLING, never recapture: every screenshot directory
carries a README stating what the images validated, the commit they were captured at, and
any known divergence since. That is mechanically checkable (the DocPolicy `Status:` gate's
own shape, one surface over), it asserts something durable rather than something that
expires hourly, and it does not cry wolf - which recapture-on-drift would, since the board's
own captures include the ambient artifact store and that store grows with every dispatch.

all. Three of four screenshot directories held no README of any kind. The gap was declared
in this file and then hit anyway, twice: a named unguarded surface is a debt, not an
excuse.*

Fix cycle ROUND 2 - your #79 probe was adversarially reviewed: REJECT, 1 Major 3 minor 2 nits. FIRST, what it verified about your work, because it went much further than the brief asked: it re-derived all five of your fixture injections with their named reds, then broke the PRODUCT itself - it built an out-of-repo copy of the checkout and injected five separate regressions into board/assemble/assemble.go (gate-role test, declaredNotObserved append, assignedSubjects, the returned-outcome branch, the gate-name source), rebuilt the real server from each, and observed exactly one named red per injection, restoring byte-identical every time. Your assertions guard the PRODUCT, not the fixture. It also tested your zero-conditions guard against the real failure mode (unsealed store: 0 passed 5 failed, guard naming record-quarantined six times plus all-records-quarantined), audited debris across fourteen runs including three concurrent and one forced mid-suite failure (zero directories, zero binaries, zero orphans, a developer's board on 4600 untouched while your probe bound 127.0.0.1:53991), and ruled your cross-platform handling clean - the 2026-07-24 ubuntu-leg Major class does not repeat. Both your friction entries were opened and tested; entry 1 reproduced verbatim.

READ THE VERDICT IN FULL, READ-ONLY: C:\Users\Chris\git\starcar\artifacts\reviews\2026-07-27-probe-79-review-r1-REJECT.md (landed after your branch was cut, not in your worktree).

Work in your same worktree C:\Users\Chris\git\starcar-wt\car-probe-79 on car/probe-79, base = your own HEAD c1c4d2dcee4023f721f2d5d433fe3bc2f3583dc1 (verify first, tree clean, STOP if not). Commit locally, NEVER push. Every finding here is a documentation defect in a durable artifact - no mechanism change is required or wanted; do NOT alter the assertions the reviewer just proved sound.

THE FINDINGS:

1. R1-M1 (MAJOR, Law 1, the only binding one) - your WHY-THIS-EXISTS header says "Today nothing asserts that join mechanically: the existing Go tests (board/assemble/assemble_test.go) cover Assemble() in isolation with constructed fold.Output/store.Record values, never the real server reading a real store over HTTP." That is false. board/server/wireschema_test.go:20-152 writes a PLAN-shaped manifest with car and gate members plus records as REAL FILES on disk (writeRecord at board/server/poll_test.go:23-32 calls os.WriteFile into t.TempDir()), runs srv.PollOnce (board/server/poll.go:253's real store scan through fold and assemble), and asserts the gates lane has exactly one gate with RecordDir and Findings (:129-137) and the trains lane has one train with two manifest tickets and carA's RecordDir (:112-123). It passes today - the reviewer observed PASS in 0.02s. Open that file yourself and verify before rewriting. Issue #79's own text carries the ACCURATE narrower claim ("no test drives the real server over a real store and asserts the four rendered properties TOGETHER") and your landing flattened it into an absolute. Rewrite the paragraph to name wireschema_test.go by path, state precisely what it DOES assert and what it does NOT (real HTTP /api/snapshot, the verdict word and gate name verbatim, per-member role/state/outcome, declaredNotObserved, assigned:true, and the zero-conditions guard - together, from a pwsh-sealed store). The reviewer's point stands: the honest version makes your case STRONGER, not weaker.

2. R1-m1 (minor) - line 45-46 says "the four quoted red messages" and then enumerates five injections (a) through (e); your commit message says five. Five is correct. A record that miscounts its own evidence invites a reader to assume one was dropped.

3. R1-m2 (minor) - your header (and the conductor's brief, which was WRONG and has since been corrected on dev) treats scripts/probes as not yet wired into CI. It is: .github/workflows/ci.yml's "Run substrate-floor probes" step runs Invoke-Pester -Path ./scripts/probes on both matrix legs and exits 1 on failure, roughly 49 lines BEFORE "Set up Go". So your suite - which needs a Go toolchain - depends on the runner image's own Go rather than a set-up one, and board/go.mod's go 1.26 against the images' 1.24.13 makes GOTOOLCHAIN auto-download fire (reviewer measured: a toolchain fetch plus ~16.6s cold build per run; simulated no-Go gives Passed=0 Failed=5, a hard red rather than a skip). Add ONE disclosure line to the header stating this dependency and where it runs. Do NOT edit ci.yml - the step-ordering decision is the conductor's and will be made after observing the real cost at merge.

4. R1-m3 (minor) - the seal is Law-6 correct but is NOT a guarded property: the reviewer replaced the digest with sha256 plus sixty-four zeros and the suite stayed 5 passed / 0 failed, because nothing in board/ recomputes it (board/store/store.go:131 declares Integrity only; schema/starcar-artifact.schema.json:100-104 pattern-checks the shape alone). Your Law-6 comment sits directly over the sealing helper and reads as though the hash were load-bearing. Add one sentence scoping it: this suite pins the JOIN, never the SEAL, so a canonicalisation change would not red here.

5. R1-n1 (nit) - the typedRecord field enumeration claims "every field Produce-Artifact.ps1 writes" and omits producer, which your own fixture writes and which typedRecord declares.

""      -> null -> "sweepsubject"      false -> null -> "sweepsubject"
null    -> null -> "sweepsubject"      NaN   -> null -> "sweepsubject"
real handle "sweep-task-r1" -> "sweep-task-r1" -> "sweep-task-r1"
```
There is no falsy string that is a meaningful task-id, so nothing meaningful changed — and `||` is *strictly safer* than `??` for the type-violation cases (`0`/`false`/`NaN`), which `??` would have rendered as literal `"0"`/`"false"`/`"NaN"` labels.

**Observation, deliberately NOT raised as a finding:** a whitespace-only `" "` is truthy and still renders a blank-looking label. I checked reachability before deciding: `Envelope.psm1:138` `.TrimEnd()` + `:154` `IsNullOrEmpty → $null` means an all-whitespace task-id never reaches a record. It is *less* reachable than the `""` case I raised, which was already only a minor. Raising it would be ratcheting, so I am recording it, not charging it.

`docs/screenshots/2026-07-26-view-28-12-candidates/README.md:21-23`:

**I opened the image.** The `#12` ticket link renders as a real anchor (visibly underlined under the train title). The health-trend badges render (`▼ converged (3→0)`, `● stalled (3→4→4)`). Confirmed from the gate's own header: *"NOT CAUGHT: an in-range shifted citation... that class stays review-attention-tier."* So the gap you're circling is documented in the tool that would catch it.

**Your instinct is right, but it targets a different class than the one I described — and yours is the one with a mechanism available.**

Sort today's Majors into two piles:

**Pile A — claims about pre-existing artifacts nobody opened** (the three I named). A doc-clearance claim over an unopened directory; a caption asserting what an image shows; a header asserting what a test doesn't cover. Writing these later wouldn't have helped — the artifact existed the whole time and was never looked at. Timing isn't the variable.

**Pile B — documentation invalidated by its own change, mid-flight.** This is yours, and it cost two Majors on the #69/#71 train alone: `lanes.js` cited `snapshot.go:41-45`, and the same commit's four-line insertion pushed the target out of range. Then the fix commit wrote `"(line 141)"` for a target its *own* +51-line insertion moved to 192 — false at the instant of commit. Both are exactly "documentation written before the change settled." Your proposal would have caught both.

**Where I'd push back on the literal form:** deferring all documentation to the end is how documentation stops getting written. "We'll do the docs at the end" has a well-known ending, and it fights the same-commit discipline that currently makes docs land at all. The version that keeps the benefit without the risk is a **final reconciliation pass**: draft whenever you like, but before committing, every documentation claim is re-verified against the *final* state of the change. Same insight, no deferral risk.

**And here's the part worth acting on** — Pile B has a tractable gate, because the repo already mandates the remedy and keeps violating it: *cite by symbol, not by line, when the file is one you're editing.* That rule is written down (it's in `gating-matrix.md`, paid for twice), and it's mechanically checkable in a way "did the author look at the PNG" never will be: **you have the diff, and you have the citations — reject any new line-number citation pointing into a file the same commit modifies.** No judgment call, no false positives against untouched files, and it extends a gate that already runs in CI rather than inventing one.

That converts the attention-tier rule into a mechanism for the exact case where line citations rot, while leaving legitimate citations into stable files alone.

Want me to file that as a ticket? And separately — Pile A stays unguarded under this, which I think is honest to admit rather than paper over: the only lever I see there is requiring evidentiary captions to *cite* the test or source that proves the claim, which the citation resolver could then verify exists. That's weaker (it proves a citation resolves, not that the claim is true), so I'd want your read before treating it as more than a half-measure.

Filed as #82, parked with your reasoning attached — including the note that it should only be built if it still looks like it earns its keep after you've settled the wider question.

On the concern itself: **it deserves support, not reassurance.** Here's the sharpest version of today's evidence, both directions.

**The gates earned their keep on substance.** The #69/#71 round-2 review caught a density regression that doubled the height of *every* dispatch row and cropped rows mid-line — user-visible, measured, on the exact surface this project exists to demonstrate. #79's reviewer proved a probe actually catches product regressions by breaking the real server five ways. A car's honest stop stopped me putting a Go-only field into a two-implementation conformance contract. The morning probe killed a design train that would have specified mechanisms that already existed. None of that is ceremony.

**But there's a specific signal I'd flag, and it's the one your instinct is picking up:** the process has started generating the artifacts it then finds defects in. That screenshot README exists *only* because a Major demanded it. Its caption then became the next Major. That's a closed loop with the shop's own output as input — and #75, a small feature that swaps a hash for a human label, is now on round three, where rounds two and three found nothing but prose accuracy in documents the process itself required.

**My candidate diagnosis is severity calibration, not ceremony volume** — and I hold it loosely, because it collides with something load-bearing. The right-sizing rule already says a coverage-class change takes one car and one reviewer; #75 got three rounds because *any Major forces a round*, and documentation-accuracy findings are being scored at Major — the same tier as a wire-contract break. The lever would be tiering a false caption below Major unless the falsehood would change what someone does. **The collision:** Law 1 says a confident falsehood on any surface is the cardinal failure, full stop. Downgrading falsehoods by consequence is a real weakening of the thing the whole shop is built around. I don't think I should resolve that tension — it's exactly the kind of definitional call that's yours.

**The practical note:** you don't have to decide now. #75's round 3 is running under a cap. If it returns another documentation Major, the cap sends it to you rather than a round 4 — and that's the natural moment to ask the right-sizing question against a live case instead of in the abstract. If it returns clean, the question stays open but stops being urgent.

One last thing, said as accounting rather than comfort: a showcase that records a process discovering its own limits is a better demonstration than one that looks frictionless. Today's record has real catches *and* real overhead in it, attributed and measured. That's worth more than a curated version — but it's only worth it if you actually get to decide where the line sits, which is what you're doing now.

content.text:
That's a genuinely good instinct, and one half of it is better than what we have. Let me separate the halves, because they pull in opposite directions on your complexity concern.

**The half that works: pinning the coordinate to a hash makes the claim permanently true.** `dom-writer.js:141 @ 256d8d5` cannot rot — at that commit, line 141 really was that line, forever. It's a paper citation with an edition number. And it has a property nothing else here has: **it's permanently machine-verifiable.** A gate can check "at hash X, does file Y line N contain Z" via git, once, and the answer never changes. A HEAD-relative citation has to be re-verified on every commit, which is exactly why ours rot.

**The cost, and it's the one your complexity worry should weigh:** a hash-pinned citation stops rotting but starts requiring archaeology. A reader at HEAD following `:141 @ 256d8d5` has to check out an old commit to see what was meant. It's durably true and decreasingly useful — the citation survives, the *reader* pays.

**Which is why symbol-form beats it wherever a symbol exists.** "`renderBoard` clears `root.textContent`" has no coordinate at all: it can't drift, needs no hash, and resolves instantly at any commit. That's already the repo's mandated form, and it's *less* machinery than your proposal, not more. So for the two Majors that started this, symbol-form is both the cheaper and the better fix.

**Where your idea genuinely wins is the gap symbol-form can't cover:** citations into things with no symbol — a line of prose in a design doc, a config value, a data fixture. Those have nothing stable to name, and today they get a bare line number that rots silently. Hash-pinning is strictly better there. And the repo already has a primitive version: the citation gate honors a `historical coordinate` marker as an author-invoked opt-out. Your proposal is essentially "formalize that, and add the hash so it's checkable" — which is a real improvement on an existing escape hatch.

**The half I'd drop: the manual supersede/deprecate chain.** That's a hand-maintained mirror of something git already holds perfectly — `git log -L` will tell you exactly what happened to that line since the pinned commit, with no chain to write, no chain to forget, and no chain to get wrong. Maintaining a deprecation trail in comments alongside git's own is the second-copy pattern that has bitten this repo before. Git *is* the supersession record; the pin is just the entry point into it.

So the clean version, and it's fewer moving parts than what you sketched: **symbol form where a symbol exists; hash-pinned coordinate where none does; git for the history, never a hand-written chain.** That's one rule with one exception and no maintenance burden.

Want me to fold that into #82? It sharpens the ticket considerably — it stops being "reject line citations into edited files" and becomes "citations resolve by symbol, or by pinned hash where no symbol exists," which is a rule you can state in one sentence and check mechanically.

**The checkpoint idea doesn't work, and the problem it was solving doesn't exist. Both measured:**

**The checkpoint branch can't answer the question.** It holds 2,208 files, and every one is `transcript.jsonl` / `full.jsonl` / `metadata.json` / `prompt.txt` / `content_hash.txt` under content-addressed directories. **Zero source files** — I grepped for any `.go`, any `board/` path, `dom-writer` specifically: nothing. It's a record of *conversations*, not of *code*. You can't resolve "what did line 141 contain" from a session transcript, so it can't serve as a citation target for source.

**And hash-pinned citations need no checkout at all** — that premise was the thing worth testing:

```
git show 256d8d5:board/web/js/dom-writer.js  →  line 141:
  root.textContent = ''; // clear() without needing a real DOM API for it
```
Working tree clean, HEAD unmoved. One command, no checkout, no branch switch. And the follow-up is better still — `git log -L 141,141:...` printed the line's entire history in one shot, and it *literally shows the drift that caused the Major*: `256d8d5` → `3fa9b21` → `8073f0b`. The tool that would diagnose the defect already exists and takes one command.

So the friction you were routing around isn't there. Git resolves pinned coordinates read-only and cheaply; that's what `git show` and `git log -L` are for.

**Where the checkpoints genuinely belong, though** — and this is worth keeping from your instinct: they're the right store for **why**, not **what**. Git tells you what the code was at a commit. The checkpoint tells you what conversation produced it, including the reasoning and the rejected alternatives that never reach a commit message. That division is real and we already lean on it: the friction mine this morning recovered four incidents from transcripts that existed nowhere else. Worth remembering as complementary provenance, not as a citation target for code.

Verified, and the answer has two parts — one that lets you off the hook, and one where **your instinct found a real design flaw before it shipped.**

**Not a bug, and the board is being honest.** Dispatched records carry no `task_id` — only returned ones do, because the shop-minted handle is echoed back in the agent's envelope. `#75` scoped the dispatched half out explicitly and deferred it here. So there is genuinely no human name to render for in-flight work yet.

**But you've caught something the design gets wrong**, and it's exactly why seeing it in flight was worth insisting on. A row whose identity *changes* mid-lifecycle — hash while running, task-id once returned — is a Law 1 problem on a board whose thesis is glanceable truth. Worse, I checked what `#76` would do about it as currently briefed, and **it doesn't fix it**: I told the car to amend a member by *replacing* the task-id with the real dispatch id, which means after amendment the human name is gone and the trains lane shows hashes too. Same flaw, one lane over.

The obvious alternative is blocked, and it's worth knowing why: stamping `task_id` at dispatch would mean parsing the free-text prompt, and `Produce-Artifact.ps1` already carries a landed ruling against exactly that — it was considered and rejected for the budget-override case as "the brittle mechanism this fix cycle's brief warns against." The launch payload has no structured field to read it from.

**The fix your observation implies is cleaner than either:** a member carries **both** — declared with its `task_id`, and amendment *adds* the real `subject` rather than replacing it. Then the board has a stable human name across the whole lifecycle plus the join key, and an in-flight dispatch can be named from its plan membership instead of waiting to return. The schema permits it (member objects don't forbid extra properties).

The car is building replace-semantics right now, so I'm sending that correction while it's cheap.

Verified: `Train` carries ID, Title, Cars, DeclaredNotObserved, Tickets — **no state field at all.** So let me correct the polarity, then say why your term is still worth having.

**The flip is at *return*, not dispatch.** The actual sequence:

- **Before dispatch** — no record exists, so the row isn't on the board at all.
- **At dispatch** — a `dispatched` record appears carrying only the runtime hash.
- **At return** — the `returned` record carries the task-id, and the row flips to a human name.

So the hash period is precisely *while the car is running* — which is the worst possible window, because that's exactly when you're watching the board to see what's happening. That's what you were reacting to.

**"Boarding" is a good word, and it names something real — but it's a train-level *state*, not a car-level *identity*.** Those are different jobs and you need both:

- A train whose members are all declared and none dispatched is genuinely "boarding" — cars listed, nothing departed. That's derivable *today* from data the board already has (`declaredNotObserved` covering the whole consist), and it would give the trains lane something honest to say about a train that exists but hasn't moved. Right now such a train renders as a consist with an empty car list, which is truthful but says nothing.
- But it doesn't give the in-flight *row* a name. "Boarding" is a state word; `ad9b6a…` still needs to read as `tooling-76-car-r1`. That's what the both-identities amendment does — once a member carries its task-id permanently, the manifest knows the human name of a dispatch that hasn't returned yet.

They compose nicely: **boarding** describes the train, **manifest membership** names the cars, and neither waits for a return.

Two design notes if we build it. It should be **derived, not stored** — a train's state falls out of its members' observation status, and storing it would be a second copy that can drift from the records. And the state words belong in `schema/vocab/` as data, the way `roles.json`, `kinds.json` and `outcomes.json` already work — a hardcoded state enum is the Law 7 violation this repo has caught before.

Filing it now, since a tooling idea gets a durable landing at birth rather than dying in conversation.

3. RECORD KIND (owner ruling): a ticket is its OWN kind - `kind: ticket`. Reusing `intent` is REJECTED (it would make a ticket indistinguishable from a manifest without inspecting the payload).
4. THE FOLD IS NOT INVOLVED (measured): freight reads raw records in `board/assemble` the way `manifestPayload` does. **A car that finds itself editing `board/fold` has gone off-contract and must HONEST-STOP.**

THE MEASURED STARTING POINT, from the conductor's probe (re-read it on the ticket; do not repeat it): a `kind: ticket` record with a `ticket` payload key LANDS (validates, integrity verifies, not quarantined), surfaces a NOMINAL `discovery: kind: ticket` because the kind vocabulary does not yet list it, and raises `record-unrecognised-fields` at needs-attention because the `ticket` key is not in the known key-set. Nothing reaches a lane, because freight is dark and has no `data` key.

YOUR SCOPE:
1. **schema/vocab/kinds.json** - add `ticket`. Values are DATA, never a schema enum (the file's own comment says why). WATCH the nominal `discovery` resolve when you do - do not assume it; that is a cheap, real non-vacuity observation.
2. **The `ticket` payload key** added to the wire schema and to every typed decoder's known key-set, following the manifest's own precedent verbatim: schema/starcar-manifest.schema.json describes the manifest key as "The single new top-level key (design DR3-1 item 4: ONE key added to the wire schema and every typed decoder's known key-set, so D17's unknown-field disclosure never fires on a well-formed manifest)". 3. **The adapter** - a script (scripts/, pwsh, following the shape of the existing producer scripts) that reads project 6's Backlog+Todo items and writes/updates `kind: ticket` records into the store, sealed with scripts/Artifact.psm1's `Get-Sha256Hex` over the compact canonical body EXACTLY as scripts/Produce-Artifact.ps1 does. Board GraphQL coordinates are on #84 and in the conductor's checkpoint; derive the project/field ids fresh rather than hardcoding stale ones (they regenerate on any options mutation - this repo has a scar for that).
4. **A freight path in board/assemble** reading raw ticket records, plus the wire payload shape in schema/yard-snapshot.schema.json alongside dispatchesPayload/gatesPayload/trainsPayload, plus a client renderer in board/web.
5. **board/server/laneregistry.go** - freight moves from `dark` to `live`. laneregistry_test.go's completeness guard must still pin all five lanes.

**THE HARDEST REQUIREMENT, AND THE ONE THE REVIEW WILL AIM AT - staleness and absence (Law 1).** Once freight is `live`, an EMPTY lane is ambiguous and that ambiguity is a confident falsehood. You must distinguish, on the rendered surface, at minimum:
- the adapter has NEVER RUN (no ticket records exist at all) - the lane must NOT read as "the queue is empty";
- the adapter RAN and the queue is GENUINELY EMPTY;
- the adapter's data is STALE (it last ran long ago) - and freshness must derive from the records' own `at`, not from wall-clock hope.
Decide how a FAILED adapter run surfaces (a written record? a condition? nothing?) and state your reasoning on the page. "No equipment on this lane" was honest for a dark lane; it is NOT automatically honest for a live one.

NON-VACUITY (#40), mandatory and the review will demand it: drive a REAL browser against the REAL served board and observe EACH of the three states above rendering DISTINCTLY. Report the observed text and computed values, not a pass/fail. Follow board/web/test/browser-dispatch-row-geometry.test.js's pattern (playwright the LIBRARY inside plain `node --test`, real Go binary, real scratch store). Also run that geometry test yourself and confirm no regression - this repo paid three rounds for a density defect on the dispatches lane.

STANDING RULES: cite #84 as bare `#84` in every new file and unit of consequence; never edit a data fixture to satisfy citation (sibling README or consuming test instead). Citations into files you edit use SYMBOL form, never line numbers (two Majors paid for that class). DOCUMENTATION RANKS EQUAL TO CODE, same commit: docs/design/2026-07-21-v0-yard-skeleton-design.md's section 7 lists this adapter as out-of-scope with a trigger that has now FIRED - true that row rather than leaving it saying freight is deferred (a satisfied trigger left in the deferred voice is a lying canary this repo corrected twice on 2026-07-27); also check the lane registry's own comment ("freight is dark (no adapter...)"), docs/specs/2026-07-23-yard-board-spec.md, and any doc enumerating lane positions. Derive suite baselines at 51fb403 BEFORE editing and report post-change arithmetic (recent finals for cross-check only, never a substitute for your own run: Pester scripts/tests 223 passed / 0 failed / 4 skipped attached, scripts/probes 29/29, Go board 98 PASS, node board/web 225/225 with node_modules present). Honest stops are SUCCESS outcomes.

FINAL REPORT: the adapter's exact invocation (the command a conductor would run); each of the three absence/staleness states with the OBSERVED rendered text from a real browser; per-hop red evidence quoted; suite arithmetic; deviations. # ADJUDICATION 4 — the derived binding. **The mechanism is sound; the lifecycle enumeration is incomplete.**

D5 is the strongest thing in this document. Because the binding is *derived at assemble time* rather than *written at some moment*, it is order-free: a returned record landing before its manifest is minted still binds. That dissolves a class of race the two rejected shapes both carried. Credit where it is due.

Lifecycle events I enumerated and checked against the document:

| Event | Covered? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Two members share a handle in one manifest | **Yes**, deferred + Q5 | §6 row + §10 Q5; correctly notes JSON Schema cannot express uniqueness over a computed key |
| Dispatch returns with a handle no manifest declares | **Yes** | D7, §6 row, V9 |
| One handle → two records (crash re-dispatch) | **Yes** | D9, V8, PR-3 measured |
| One record → two members / two manifests | **Yes, and partly already built** | `assemble.go:169-187` already raises `manifest-membership-collision`; D9 generalizes it |
| Handle reused across trains | **Yes** — same as above | |
| Fix-cycle rounds | **Yes** — D1 mints a new task-id per round (`-r1`, `-r2`) | |
| Manifest superseded, consist GROWS | **Yes** | P4, the six landed records (1→2→4→6→8→10, verified) |
| Manifest superseded, consist SHRINKS (member removed mid-flight) | **NOT ENUMERATED** | P4 names only growth; §6 has no row. Behaviour is inherited-unchanged (removed member's record flips to unattributed → D7 discloses it), so honest — but undesigned |
| **`presumed-lost`** | **NOT ENUMERATED ANYWHERE** | see below |

**`presumed-lost` is the gap worth naming.** It is a first-class kind (`schema/vectors/valid-presumed-lost.json`, `Detect-Dispatches.ps1:163-164` precedence `returned > presumed-lost > dispatched`), it is the record for the #32 killed-session class the owner's ruling says the manifest exists to make detectable, and **it carries no `task_id`** — `Produce-Artifact.ps1:358` writes `task_id` only when `$Kind -eq 'returned'`, and the canonical vector has none. Under D5 a presumed-lost record therefore falls back to `subject` (a runtime id) and binds to no member. §5.1's table lists it in the dispatch stream and §5.2's three epochs, §6's failure table, and §5.6's V-set never mention it again. Under D6/D7 the board would still render two true statements, so it is not a Law-1 hole — but the design's own headline use case (the killed session) routes through a record kind the document never traces. It belongs in §5.2 and §6 explicitly, and D8's stamping question ("does a presumed-lost record inherit its dispatched sibling's `task_id`?") is unasked.

Corpus check, read-only over the real store: **0 presumed-lost records exist today**, so nothing is broken now — this is a design-completeness finding, not a live defect. Folded into DR1-m4's class as a note rather than its own Major, because the rendering stays honest.

Corpus-wide for context: 177 returned records, 96 carry `task_id`; 83 dispatched records, **0** carry `task_id`.

**Does the fallback protect RENDERING and not merely validation? YES — measured (my PR-4a above).** A legacy-shaped manifest through the real board renders both members bound with liveness, `declaredNotObserved:[]`, zero conditions. Without the fallback clause those two rows would vanish from the consist while their records still sat in the store — Law 4 silent loss on a rendered surface.

The author recorded it rather than dismissing it, and V7 pins the precedence so a future change reds. That is the right handling.

**Ruling on Q4 (is the fallback worth its price?): YES, and the author's reading of NO-BACKFILL is correct, not a stretch.** Law 4 is explicit — *"a missing lane reading as 'no trains' is a lie of omission"* (`constitution.md:33-37`). A rendered train silently losing its consist is the same class one level down. The author flagged this reading as "mine, not the doctrine's literal text, and it deserves attack"; attacked, it holds.

I've listed four questions on the ticket that shouldn't be answered by a car alone, including whether precedence becomes time-aware (smaller change, possibly wrong — `presumed-lost` exists precisely so a later absence doesn't override an earlier return).

**Separately, #84's freight car landed** and its review is running: Go 108/108, node 234/234, Pester 235, three fault injections, and the three Law 1 absence states each observed distinctly in a real browser. The reviewer is briefed to find the *fourth* state the car didn't enumerate, and to rule on two design decisions the car made on its own — that a failed adapter run writes nothing (so failure reads as staleness), and that ticket records are overwritten in place and deleted on departure, which loses history in a repo whose thesis is an append-only record.

`board/server/poll.go:365-367` sets `s.lastGoodAsOf["freight"] = newLastGood` on **every** successful scan, and `:398-402` sets `s.lastGoodLaneData["freight"] = assembled.Freight` unconditionally — regardless of whether a `ticket-sync` heartbeat exists. `:330-334` then serves that as the `failed` variant's `LastGoodAsOf`.

**Measured, real browser, real Go binary** (probe: empty scratch store → poll → `renameSync` the store away):

```
BEFORE store loss: freightSecondary = "not yet polled"          register-in-progress
AFTER  store loss: freightSecondary = "source failed (...) - showing last good from 2026-07-27T17:10:36Z"
                   freightBody      = "no tickets in the queue"  register-needs-attention
```

One poll earlier the board itself said the adapter had never run. It now asserts it is showing the last good freight queue, and that it was empty. This is precisely the collapse the issue forbids: *"An empty lane that silently means 'we do not know' is the confident-falsehood class this board exists to prevent."*

The reuse is unexamined and the comment above it proves the car knew the distinction mattered — `poll.go:304-314` argues `freightFreshnessVal` is "DELIBERATELY a separate value… never a reuse", while the `lastGood` bookkeeping 50 lines below **is** a reuse of a lane whose definition of "good" the car deliberately made different. For dispatches/gates/trains a successful scan genuinely *is* good data (DR3-5a honest-empty); for freight it explicitly is not.

`TestPollOnceFreightRetainsLastGoodOnScanFailure` (`poll_test.go:203-233`) cannot catch this — its poll-1 store seeds a heartbeat at `:205`, so it only exercises the case where freight really did have good data.

### R1-M2 — Heartbeat absent + tickets present renders "not yet polled" beside the tickets, reachable by a real adapter failure

`computeFreightFreshness` returns `never-polled` at `poll.go:547-549` purely on heartbeat absence, while `assemble.go:235` populates `Freight.Tickets` from any `kind=ticket` records regardless. Nothing reconciles the two.

```
4 Freight  the inbound ticket queue  Live  not yet polled  #84 first ticket Backlog
```

The secondary line says the adapter has never run; the body shows a ticket only the adapter could have written. No board condition fires. This is a HAVAGLANCE failure — a single glance transmits two contradictory facts.

This is **not hypothetical**: it is the direct consequence of the car's own heartbeat-written-LAST ordering (`Sync-Freight.ps1:184-185`). | S2 ran, empty | `fresh` | nominal | no tickets ✅ |

No screenshot README was touched by this commit and the commit message never mentions screenshots. The remedy the template prescribes is not recapture — it is a README stating the divergence. `scripts/Sync-Freight.ps1:35-38`:

> *"a failed run (the gh call throws, a write fails) writes NOTHING - not even a 'we tried and failed' record - and exits nonzero."*

4. **R1-M4 (Law 1) - your adapter's own documented contract is measurably false.** `scripts/Sync-Freight.ps1:35-38` says "a failed run ... writes NOTHING - not even a 'we tried and failed' record - and exits nonzero." content.text:
That's a better question than the one I asked, and answering it honestly changes the shape of the option.

**What it actually buys — three things, in descending order of realness:**

**1. It freezes the binding against derivation drift.** The derived binding is recomputed on every poll, so if the join rule ever changes, *history re-renders differently*. A stored id says "this is what was true at the time" and can't be retroactively rewritten by a later rule change. This repo already ruled exactly this way once, for exactly this reason — `Produce-Artifact.ps1` stamps the budget at dispatch, with the comment: *"The promise freezes into history at departure; a later policy change never rewrites in-flight liveness verdicts."* Same argument, different field. That's a real precedent, not an analogy I'm stretching.

**2. Reverse lookup for forensics.** Given a runtime id from a fault log, a transcript, or a CI failure — *what was it doing, and which plan slot did it serve?* Today that needs a scan-and-derive across manifests. This morning's friction mine did precisely that kind of lookup, by hand, through the checkpoint branch.

**3. Survival when the records don't.** The binding is derived *from the dispatch records*. When #68's archive retrieval lands and records move out of the hot store, the derivation loses its inputs and the pairing evaporates. A stored id keeps the plan's memory of what actually ran, in the plan itself.

**And here's the part the design missed, which your reframe exposes:** it priced the enrichment option as reintroducing the vigilance dependency — a human remembering to amend per dispatch. But that cost comes from *who writes it and when*, not from storing it. If the **board derives the binding and a tool freezes it** — no human in the loop — there's no vigilance at all. That's a third shape neither the design nor my question offered: **derive it, then freeze it.** Machine-written, so P7 doesn't apply; stored, so it survives rule changes and archiving.

**My honest read on whether to do it now:** none of the three is biting today. Nothing is broken for want of it, no forensic question has failed, and #68 hasn't landed. NIRTS says that's an argument for *not* building it yet — but the freezing argument is strong enough, and precedented enough, that "forbid it entirely" may be the wrong permanent posture even if it's the right immediate one.

Which suggests the useful ruling might be narrower than allow-or-forbid: **keep the strict form in the schema now, and record the derive-then-freeze shape as the named reopening path with its trigger** — the first time a derivation change would have rewritten history, or the first archive-retrieval question we can't answer. That keeps the format artifact small, keeps Law 6 clean today, and stops a future agent from reading "D2 forbids it" as a settled fence with no story attached.

Want me to put it to the design that way, or does the freezing argument land hard enough for you that you'd rather have it in the schema from the start?

The durable habit going into briefs: *verify a restore against HEAD by diff or hash, never against your memory of what the file held* — and prefer `git checkout` over hand-rolled backups, since git already knows the correct content.

The reviewer is briefed to rule whether anything in the final commit rests on evidence gathered during that window, which is the same question its design-review counterpart faced today about a vacuous injection.

Partly — and you're right about the part that matters, but it reopens something the design specifically killed, so let me lay the fork out rather than just agree.

**Where your gut is exactly right.** There's one case where the join genuinely doesn't exist anywhere: a **Claude-family dispatch that's in flight.** Its record carries a runtime hash and no handle; the manifest carries a handle and no runtime id; nothing connects them. The link lives only in my head at the moment I dispatch. For *that* case, storing the runtime id is **not** a second copy of a derivable fact — it's the only copy, which defeats the Law 6 objection the design leans on. That's also precisely the gap behind both bugs you reported: the hash-titled in-flight rows, and cars that never show they're back out.

**Where it gets complicated.** The design attacked the premise *"the manifest must name the runtime id at all"* and found it **false** — and the inversion, the record naming its plan, dissolved more of the problem than anything else it tried. Its answer to the same gap is D8: the producer stamps the handle **into the dispatch record** from a field the launch payload already carries. Same link, recorded from the other side.

So the real question your gut opens isn't *store or don't* — it's **which direction the pointer runs, and who writes it:**

- **Plan → runtime** (yours): the manifest gets a ref to the agent id. Works for both runtime families and survives re-dispatch. Cost: **someone has to write it at dispatch**, which is the amendment step the design spent a whole premise killing — if I forget, the member is silently unbound.
- **Runtime → plan** (the design's D8): the record carries the handle. Cost: it depends on me writing the handle into the launch description, which is also a convention — but a lighter one, because it rides a field that's populated on every dispatch anyway.

**The honest asymmetry:** both need a human to do something right at dispatch time. D8's version is something I'm already doing; yours is a separate step *after* the fact. That's the whole of the difference, and it's smaller than the design's framing makes it sound.

**One thing that doesn't rescue it:** derive-and-freeze — the shape I floated earlier — works nicely for the epochs where the join *is* derivable, but it can't help here. There's nothing to derive for an in-flight Claude dispatch, so freezing gives you nothing.

My read, stated as a lean rather than a recommendation: your instinct is sound and the gap is real, but I'd want the pointer **written by a machine, not by me** — otherwise we've traded a derivation for a vigilance dependency, and this shop has a scar for exactly that trade. If there's a way for the producer to write the manifest ref at dispatch (it knows the agent id; it would need to know the train), that's your version with the cost removed. Whether that's feasible I genuinely don't know — it'd need a probe.

Want me to probe that before you rule? It's the difference between your shape being clean and your shape carrying the one cost the design was built to avoid.

**Both probed, and the first result corrects something I told you.**

**Probe 1 — can a machine write the pointer?** The producer's payload at dispatch carries `tool_response.agentId`, so the runtime id is available either way. But **nothing in it identifies a train, a ticket, or a manifest** — no such field exists, and parsing the prompt is ruled out. The only conductor-authored channel is `description`.

Which means: **the input requirement is identical for both directions.** Whether the producer stamps the handle *into the record* or writes a manifest *ref back to the plan*, it needs the same one thing — me putting a structured handle in `description`. Once that's there, either direction is machine-writable.

So the vigilance asymmetry I described to you doesn't exist. I told you your shape was "a separate step after the fact" carrying the amendment cost the design killed. Measured, it isn't — the producer can do it, on the same single convention D8 already needs. That was my reasoning, not a measurement, and it was wrong.

**Probe 2 — the issue as index.** Your instinct is already satisfied, one level down: **all 105 shop handles in the store encode their issue numbers**, including trains spanning several (`register-35-36-37-car-r1`, `tooling-50-32-car-r4`). The handle *is* a structured derivation of the issue — `area – issue(s) – role – round`.

But the bare issue number can't be the join key, for two independent reasons: it's **too coarse** (one issue spawns many dispatches — car r1, review r1, car r2…) and it's **not train-unique** (one train spans several issues). The handle is the issue-derived key at the right granularity, and it's what the design already uses as member identity. So the manifest genuinely does derive from the issue — it just needs the round and role that the issue alone can't supply.

**What's left of Q1 is now much narrower.** Not "does it cost vigilance" (no, if the producer writes it) and not "should the issue be the index" (it already is). Just: **should the plan point at the runtime, or the runtime point at its plan?** Both are machine-writable from the same input, so this is a pure direction call — Law 6 and legibility, not cost.

Your gut said plan → runtime. The design's premise attack said the inversion dissolved more. With the cost argument now removed from my side of the scale, I don't think I should be the one to break that tie.
ah ok so we can go with the probe 1 idea and drop probe 2's idea?

Not quite — and the distinction matters because it's about to go into a design.

**Neither probe was an idea; both were questions**, and both came back in your favour:

- **Probe 1** didn't propose anything. It *removed an objection* to your shape — I'd claimed plan→runtime carried a vigilance cost that runtime→plan didn't, and that turned out to be false.
- **Probe 2** didn't propose an alternative either. It found your issue intuition **already satisfied**: the handle *is* the issue, structured (`area – issue(s) – role – round`). That's not dropped — it's the thing that makes either direction work at all, because it's the key at the right granularity.

The only thing measurement ruled out is using the **bare issue number** as the join key — too coarse (one issue, many dispatches) and not train-unique (one train, many issues). Your underlying instinct that the issue is the source stands and is already built in.

**What's still undecided is the one thing neither probe touched: direction.**

- **Plan → runtime** (your gut): the manifest member gains a ref to the runtime id. The plan keeps a durable record of what actually served each slot; it survives archiving and derivation changes.
- **Runtime → plan** (the design's D8): the dispatch record carries the handle. The plan stays pure declaration; the binding is always recoverable from records alone.

Both are now machine-writable from the same input, so cost is off the table. What's left is Law 6 and legibility — one stores a fact in two places that can drift, the other keeps a single source but leaves the plan silent about what happened.

That's a genuine judgment call and it's yours. If you want to rule now, say which direction and I'll fold it into the design's Q1 and brief the format car. If you'd rather see it in flight first — which is what you asked for with #76 and it paid off twice — we can leave Q1 open and let the format car build everything that doesn't depend on it.
ok so my gut direction is the one that doesn't say what hte plan did, right?

Backwards — and that's my fault, my last sentence paired the trade-offs in an order that didn't map cleanly onto the options.

**Your gut is the one where the plan DOES say what happened.**

- **Plan → runtime (your gut):** the manifest member records the runtime id that served it. Open the plan, and it tells you what actually ran in each slot. The plan speaks.
- **Runtime → plan (the design's):** the plan only ever declares intent. It never learns what served it; you reconstruct that from the dispatch records every time. The plan stays silent.

The costs attach the same way round: yours keeps a durable answer in the plan but stores a fact that also lives in the records (the drift risk), while the design's keeps one source of truth but means the plan can never answer "what ran here" on its own — and if records are archived or the derivation rule changes, that answer changes with them.

So your instinct was for the *talkative* plan. Which is consistent with what you've been asking for all morning — you wanted trains visible in flight, and a plan that records its own history is the version that can still tell you afterward.

is it really a drift risk though? I ask it that way because once the runtime is done, it's done. THat portion of hte plan is over, and should never be written to agian. Even if it was the same ticket, on a new runtime, it would generate a new line, yes?

You're right, and I think that argument actually defeats the objection rather than just softening it.

**Drift requires that at least one copy can change after both are written.** Under your model neither can: the runtime id of a completed dispatch is a historical fact, and the record carrying it is sealed and append-only. Law 6's clause is literally *"a second copy of anything that **can** drift"* — a write-once record of a finished event isn't in that category at all. It's not a cache of a live value; it's a note of something that happened.

And it's stronger than "not a risk." It's the freezing argument from earlier, now with teeth: the *derived* binding is the one that can change, because it recomputes under whatever the join rule says today. The stored pointer is the more reliable of the two, not the more fragile. Same reasoning the budget stamp already uses — *"the promise freezes into history at departure."*

**Two things survive, and neither is drift:**

**One is a write-correctness question.** Manifest supersession replaces the *whole* record, so an amendment restates every member line — which means a later write could reintroduce a wrong value into a line that should have been closed. That's a mistake, not a divergence, and it's mechanically checkable against the record. Worth a vector; not an argument against the shape.

**The other is a premise of yours that measurement contradicts, and it matters for the spec.** You said the same ticket on a new runtime generates a new line — true for a *new* agent. But our fix cycles **resume the same agent**: the #75 car ran three rounds under one runtime id (`ae9c59ae16e969916` — one dispatched record, three returned). So a single runtime id can serve `-r1`, `-r2` and `-r3`. The pointer stays unique going plan→runtime (each member has one id), but it is **not** unique in reverse — given a runtime id, "which slot?" has several answers. That's fine for what you want it for, and it's exactly the fact behind bug #89. The format spec needs to say so rather than assume one-to-one.

So: the Law 6 objection doesn't hold, the cost objection didn't survive probe 1, and the issue-as-source instinct is already built in. What's left is the direction call, and the only remaining argument against your side just collapsed.

# FINDINGS

## **A1-M1 (Major) — PR-8's headline figure is false by the design's own stated metric, in seven places.**

§2b PR-8 (line 327) states the metric precisely: *"for every runtime `subject`, **how many distinct shop handles (`task_id`s on its `returned` records)** does it serve?"* — then answers *"**43 of 109** subjects serve MORE THAN ONE member."*

**Measured by me over the same store, by that exact definition: 26, not 43.**

```
A) distinct task_id count GT 1        : 26      <- the stated metric
B) returned-record count GT 1         : 43      <- what 43 actually counts
```

**The 17-subject gap is the opposite of the claim.** Those subjects hold **35 returned records between them, 0 carrying `task_id`** — pre-#47 fossils predating the envelope echo. They serve **zero identified members**, not "more than one". Six of the 17 are `train:board-v0` members from the legacy corpus I measured in round 1.

**Seven locations:** lines 39 (header), 327 (PR-8), 421 (D10's reason column), 995 (*"wrong on more than a third of this shop's real corpus"* — 26/109 is 24%, about a quarter), 1000 (§5.8a), 1123 (§9b), 1328 (Q9).

**Everything else in PR-8 is exact, and I want that on the record separately:** 109 subjects ✓; **76 distinct handles ✓** (unaffected, precisely because the 17 contribute none); max FIVE rounds ✓; **every multi-group has exactly one `dispatched`, 0 exceptions ✓**; and all three named exemplars exact — `ab2bd332be0eebc2c` = `tooling-65-car-r1`…`-r5` **all `SUCCESS`** ✓, `af5f0b4f753a8f9d7` = `tooling-50-32-car-r1`…`-r5` ✓, `a353ad2db7e6ad627` = `view-75-review-r1/r2/r3` ✓.

**D10 survives with a wide margin** — 26 subjects and 76 handles is ample basis, and I confirmed the mechanism directly (below). This is a correction, not a redesign.

**Class, and it is why this is Major rather than Minor:** this is DR1-M1's exact shape at the same rung — a real number answering a different question than its sentence asks — inside the section whose own opening promises *"every behavioural claim in this document is traceable to an observation rather than a reading."* The author diagnosed DR1-M1's root cause as *"a reading dressed as a measurement"*; this is one measurement dressed as another.

**Constructive: the honest statement is stronger than the false one.** *"26 subjects are MEASURED to serve more than one member; a further 17 have multiple returned records carrying no handle at all, so what they served is **unknowable**."* Unknowable provenance is an even worse thing to dereference than shared provenance — the correction reinforces D10.

## **A1-M2 (Major) — PR-8 makes an unresolved ambiguity in D5 outcome-determining, and one reading reproduces this design's own founding defect on a quarter of the store.**

§5.5 states the join over "**a record**". But a bound member's liveness, outcome and superseded history come from a **fold entry** — `board/assemble/assemble.go:110` (`dispatchBySubject[m.Subject]`, built from `fold.Output`) — and the fold keeps **exactly one entry per subject** (`board/fold/algorithm.go:154-163`, `foldDispatchSubject` returning one `DispatchEntry` per subject).

**Measured.** I wrote the real `ab2bd332be0eebc2c` shape into a scratch store — 1 `dispatched` + 5 `returned`, distinct handles, outcomes REJECT×4 then APPROVE — and ran the real board:

```
RECORDS WRITTEN: 6 under ONE subject
DISPATCH ROWS RENDERED: 1
  subject=ab2bd332be0eebc2c state=returned outcome=APPROVE taskId=tooling-65-car-r5 superseded=5
```

**Under fold-entry semantics, only `-r5` can bind.** Members `-r1`…`-r4` render *"declared, no departure bound"* **while their returned records sit in the store carrying their handles and their outcomes** — and **no condition is raised**, because the single fold entry IS assigned, to `-r5`. That is precisely PR-1's Law 1 shape — the board asserting members have not departed while holding their returned records — arriving through the fold collapse instead of through shape B, on the 26 subjects and 76 handles PR-8 just measured.

Under raw-record semantics all five bind, but then liveness and superseded history must come from somewhere the fold does not provide per member, which the design also does not specify.

**The amendment draws exactly one conclusion from PR-8 — D10, about the pointer — and never asks the same question of D5, its central mechanism.** §5.8a's own sentence applies verbatim to the binding: *"the collapse happens in the fold before any consumer sees it."* A `grep` for `fold winner` / `fold entry` / `raw record` finds the collapse addressed only for the pointer (line 1013) and for manifest supersession (line 1024).

**In scope:** PR-8 is new work introduced by this amendment, and this is its unexamined implication. The underlying fact is the one the ruling names as *"the same fact behind #89"*. **Likely a small fix:** say whether §5.5's join runs over raw records or fold entries; if fold entries, add a §6 failure row and a vector for the members a resumed agent served that the fold cannot surface.

## **A1-m1 (Minor) — a FOURTH surviving D2-strict claim, undisclosed. The sweep reports three.**

**P3, lines 177-180:** *"A structured identity … would let a member carry the binding inline. That is precisely the shape P5 kills: **it puts a runtime fact inside a plan record**, and it re-imports mutation, supersession-of-identity and ordering."*

D2′ now expressly permits a runtime fact inside a plan record, so P3's first stated ground is superseded — **the same shape as disclosed survivor (c)** (V13's *"D2 gives the manifest no runtime fact to mutate toward"*), annotated nowhere. P3's *conclusion* survives on independent grounds (D1/D3 keep identity one string; D10 keeps the pointer out of identity), so harm is bounded — but the sweep is presented as complete at three and it is four. One annotation fixes it.

*Sweep otherwise verified complete:* I grepped independently for D2-strict phrasings and the only other hits are D2 itself (correctly struck, line 419) and the two disclosed survivors.

Say it plainly, as asked.** I tested the reasoning against the real fold rather than accepting it, and the probe above is the confirmation: five rounds under one runtime id collapse to **one** row carrying round 5's outcome. The five vectors — writable, and V18's red half genuinely reds.** V18's red half is a pointer carrying `-r2`; no record subject ever carries a suffix, so a byte-verbatim comparison fails — and it usefully traps anyone re-proposing the withdrawn composite. V19 is the vector that protects the ruling and is writable (I built essentially its fixture). V20's two directions are both record-checkable. V21's NO-BACKFILL pin is right. The header's cap paragraph now reads *"Rev 3 was APPROVED (0 Major, 4 Minor; the round-2 cap did NOT fire) and merged to `dev` at `8bcaf10`"* — accurate to my verdict. **All four DR3 Minors folded**, DR3-m2 taking *both* rows I offered plus carrying my not-fix-created note forward, and DR3-m4 splitting option (ii) into (ii-a)/(ii-b) with (ii-b) priced as manufacturing an invisible dispatch and **recommended for outright rejection** rather than quietly dropped.
